subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prospect Theory in Medicine
description: A 60-second lesson on Prospect Theory in Medicine.

hook.text: Patients told a surgery has 90% survival rate agree more than those told it has 10% mortality rate. Same surgery.

buildup.text: McNeil's study showed that framing affects even life-and-death medical choices. Doctors are affected too.

discovery.text: Medical framing shifts treatment choices, vaccination rates, and screening behavior through gain/loss language.

twist.text: Ethical dilemma: should doctors frame information to guide patients toward better outcomes, or present it neutrally?

climax.text: Best practice: present both frames. '90% survive and 10% don't' gives patients the full picture in both directions.

punchline.text: In medicine, framing can save lives or cost them.

quiz.question: How does framing affect medical decisions?
options: It has no effect on patients or doctors
Survival frames increase acceptance of treatments vs mortality frames

details.summary: Medical decisions are profoundly affected by framing. Patients and doctors choose differently when outcomes are described as survival rates rather than mortality rates, even though the information is mathematically identical.
details.whyItMatters: How medical information is framed can literally be a matter of life and death. Patients may refuse beneficial treatments when framed as mortality risk but accept them when framed as survival probability.
takeaways: Survival framing increases treatment acceptance versus mortality framing
Doctors are susceptible to framing effects in treatment recommendations
Loss-framed messages are more effective for detection behaviors

faq.question: How does framing affect cancer treatment decisions?
faq.answer: A surgery with a 90 percent five-year survival rate sounds much better than one with a 10 percent five-year mortality rate. Patients are significantly more likely to choose surgery when outcomes are framed in survival terms.

faq.question: Should doctors present both frames to patients?
faq.answer: Ethical guidelines increasingly recommend presenting both gain and loss frames. Showing both the 90 percent survival rate and the 10 percent mortality rate gives patients a more complete picture and reduces the distortion from one-sided framing.
